method: luma-competitor-analysis-pro, Phase 3 (Feature Inventory), restricted to four threads (A: ranking axes & effort; B: loyalty & the first-time traveller; C: the disruption gap; D: business goal 2, the trip as a single object). Phases 1-2 are complete and were not re-run. No web browsing was performed for this phase. Every fact below was re-read from the underlying capture file it cites -- not taken on trust from CAPTURE-INDEX.json's one-line claim text -- because the index is a generated summary and the capture file is the thing that resolves a claim.

sources.capture_index_role: Superset index (121 findings across 50 capture files, 17 competitors) used to locate candidate findings per thread, per the task brief's instruction that CAPTURE-INDEX.json is the superset and WORLD.json is short by 4 rows (correction C-043). WORLD.json was not read for this artifact.

normalisations.decision: Treated as one concept throughout this file, labelled 'ranking axis'. The capture files use all four terms depending on which competitor's UI is being described (Booking.com/Expedia/Google/Airbnb: 'sort'; Kayak: 'sort tabs'; Trainline: no UI control, only a stated policy).

normalisations.merge: capture-level axis kind labels -> the six schema buckets (price / quality proxy / distance / property type / opaque default / effort-convenience)
normalisations.decision: Capture files use several near-synonymous labels for the same bucket: 'opaque_personalised' (Expedia) and 'opaque_default' (Booking.com, Google) were merged into one 'opaque default' bucket. 'effort_ease_stress_confidence', 'effort_ease_stress', 'effort_or_convenience_axes' and 'effort_duration' were all merged into one 'effort-convenience' bucket. This is a naming merge only; no axis was reclassified into a different bucket than its own capture file assigned it.

Flagged rather than silently folded in. The capture that introduces Emissions (07-flights-sort-axes-MATERIAL-CORRECTION.json) explicitly counts it inside 'effort_or_convenience_axes': 4, alongside Departure time, Arrival time and Duration. A separate, earlier capture in the same file (finding F-34, inherited from 06-flights-live-route.json) describes emissions as 'neither price, quality proxy, nor distance' without asserting it IS an effort axis -- it is a carbon/sustainability measure, not literally a measure of traveller effort. This file follows the source's own later, more considered classification (the correction capture) and places Emissions in effort-convenience, but records the tension: a chart bucketing Emissions under 'effort' is following the vendor capture's own accounting, not an independent judgement that emissions measures effort.

normalisations.merge: Kayak 'Best' (composite price+duration) axis -> counted once, toward the effort-convenience side
normalisations.decision: Kayak's own finding F-43 states 'two of three axes concern duration' -- meaning 'Best' (a composite of price AND duration) is counted on the duration/effort side, not split 0.5/0.5 across price and effort. This file preserves that whole-number counting rather than inventing a fractional split the source does not support.
Booking.com's capture uses 'Genius Level', Expedia's uses 'tier', Qatar's uses 'tier', Iberia's programme was never observed to name tiers at all (see Thread B gap). Normalised to 'tier' throughout.

NOT merged into one 'loyalty currency' concept for numeric comparison. They have different redemption mechanics (spendable currency vs automatic discount vs status-only points) and merging their numbers into one column would imply comparability the captures do not support. Kept as named, separate fields per programme.

Treated as one target concept ('disruption/passenger-rights help') for the purpose of stating whether a route exists, but the exact search-term lists differ per competitor and are preserved verbatim per entry rather than normalised to one canonical list, because the method itself changed between competitors (English terms on Iberia and Qatar; a first, WRONG-locale English sweep on American Airlines that returned a false null, corrected to Spanish terms) and collapsing the term lists would hide that method drift.

effort_convenience(4) = Departure time, Arrival time, Duration, Emissions -- matches the capture's own 'effort_or_convenience_axes': 4 exactly. See the Emissions normalisation entry above for the caveat on classifying Emissions as effort.

effort_convenience(2) = 'Best' (composite price+duration) + 'Shortest duration', matching F-43's 'two of three concern duration' exactly. 'Best' is a composite that also contains price; it is counted once, on the effort side, per the normalisation entry above -- not split.

route_from_own_navigation.verbatim: No capture runs a systematic search-term sweep of Booking.com's navigation for disruption/rights labels the way Iberia and Qatar were tested. What exists instead is a categorised site-tree listing (product lines, loyalty/account, legal/policy) with ~26 named destinations; none of the named destinations is labelled disruption, delay, cancellation, compensation or passenger rights -- the closest are 'Customer support' and 'Dispute resolution'. This is weaker evidence than a term-sweep null and must not be reported as an equivalent negative result.

contractual_liability_position.value: Discloses liability for flights specifically: 'We act solely as the Platform and are not involved in the Third-Party Terms... have no liability to you in relation to your Booking.' Most flights are provided via a Third-Party Aggregator -- liability is disclaimed at the first hop.

counter_case.value: Booking.com DOES operate a proactive disruption mechanism, but only where it holds the direct supplier relationship: for pre-booked airport transfers, travellers must give flight details 24 hours ahead 'so your Service Provider can adjust the pick-up Time if your flight is delayed.' For the flight itself, the response is to point the traveller at statutory EU 261/2004 rights in the Terms of Service, not to act.

cross_document_pattern.value: Across three first-party documents (Terms of Service, Accessibility Statement, Genius programme page), Booking.com consistently occupies an intermediary position and routes responsibility outward: flight liability to the aggregator/airline, accessibility of the actual travel experience to the supplier, and the one benefit that implies acting FOR the traveller (Genius priority support) gated behind 15 bookings in 2 years.

method_asymmetry_warning.value: The five 'route exists?' results above were NOT produced by the same method and are not safely comparable on one chart axis. Iberia's null is a three-surface, eleven-term sweep. Qatar's null is a one-surface, seven-term sweep. Booking.com's is a site-tree category read, not a sweep at all. American Airlines has two DIFFERENT results depending on which localised site is tested, and the higher-content US result was reached by URL guess, not navigation. Hopper's counter-case was found by direct navigation to a named product, not a sweep. A chart presenting these as one uniform 'disruption findability' metric across competitors would overstate how comparable the underlying tests are -- the source material itself raises this caveat explicitly for the AA/Iberia pair and it generalises to the whole set.

D.definition: What state a traveller carries across a product boundary and what is dropped. The Airbnb stays-to-Experiences date-drop is the known instance. This section searches the captures for any OTHER instance, on any competitor, and reports the count found.

known_instance.value: Airbnb: navigating from a dated Stays search (checkin 2026-11-10, checkout 2026-11-13) to Experiences produced a URL carrying NO dates. A full sweep of the 8,765-character Experiences results page for 'tu viaje', 'tu estancia', 'tu reserva', 'anadir al viaje', 'durante tu', 'itinerario' returned zero matches. This is within ONE company, one account, three inventories (stays, experiences, services) under one login.

other_instances_found.statement: Exactly one other instance of the same pattern -- trip state crossing a product boundary and arriving wrong -- was found in the capture set read for this phase.

instance.value: Trainline: a PRE-CHECKED 'Get up to 20% off stays with Genius' (Booking.com) cross-sell control in the Trainline search form, on search, opened a Booking.com hotel search in the original tab with checkin=2026-09-04, checkout=2026-09-05 -- today and tomorrow, not the travel dates the traveller had actually searched for on Trainline. The URL's own tracking label contains the word 'popunder'.

other_instances_found.why_this_counts_as_a_second_instance: Like the Airbnb case, a traveller's trip state (specifically, the dates) fails to survive a boundary crossing that a product itself initiates. It differs from the Airbnb case in two ways worth keeping distinct rather than merging: (1) it crosses a COMPANY boundary (Trainline to Booking.com) rather than a vertical boundary within one company; (2) the dates are not merely absent, they are present and WRONG (today/tomorrow), which is arguably a worse failure mode than Airbnb's silent absence.

adjacent_but_distinct_observations.value: Kayak to Iberia handoff: the full itinerary (origin, destination, dates, flight number, fare code, displayed price) IS carried across the boundary intact and verified to survive (58.25 EUR appears on both sides). What is dropped instead is BRANDING/PROVENANCE CONTEXT: the destination page contains no trace of Kayak, and the traveller immediately faces a fresh cookie-consent gate. This is NOT counted as a third 'trip-state drop' instance because the trip data itself does not drop here -- only the sense of where the traveller came from does. Recorded separately so it is not conflated with the Airbnb/Trainline pattern.

Iberia via the same Kayak handoff: the fare code Kayak passed (a Basic Economy / 'Turista Basica' fare) is presented back to the traveller as 'Has escogido la tarifa: Turista Basica' (You have chosen the fare) -- the underlying data survives the handoff accurately, but the AGENCY/DECISION context is misrepresented: the traveller did not choose this fare, Kayak's link did. Also not counted as a trip-STATE drop, since the fare code itself is carried correctly; what is misrepresented is whose decision it was.

counter_case.value: TripIt models the trip as one object precisely by refusing to sell anything: travellers forward confirmation emails from any source to plans@tripit.com and TripIt assembles them into one itinerary view. It solves the boundary-drop problem by not having boundaries of its own -- it never initiates a cross-sell or a vertical switch that could drop state, because it has no verticals to switch between, only ingestion.

not_counted_as_instances_but_relevant_co.value: Booking.com's own answer to multi-type trip attachment is three opt-in checkboxes inside the booking form (interested_flight, interested_car_rentals, interested_taxi) captured at checkout. This is a different mechanism from a boundary-crossing drop -- it is interest capture at a single moment, not a handoff between two searches -- so it is not counted as a 'drop' instance, but it is a third distinct model (alongside Airbnb's silent multi-vertical account and Trainline's pre-checked cross-sell) for how the round's competitors handle business goal 2.

D.search_method_note: This search was not a single uniform sweep across all 17 competitors and 50 capture files with one fixed term list -- no such sweep exists on disk. It was a review of every capture file that: (a) explicitly tests a cross-vertical or cross-company handoff, or (b) explicitly discusses trip state, itinerary, dates or context surviving or failing to survive a boundary. The two instances counted above are the only ones meeting that description found among the 50 capture files read for this phase.

gaps: Thread A -- accommodation: only four products have an enumerated ranking-axis count (Booking.com, Expedia, Google Travel, Airbnb). Skyscanner, Hopper, Omio, Tripadvisor and Rentalcars' accommodation/car sort controls were never opened or enumerated in the captures read for this phase. A same-vertical chart covering 'the market' would be four of at least nine accommodation-capable competitors on the roster.

Thread A -- flights: only two products have an enumerated ranking-axis count (Google Flights, Kayak). Booking.com, Expedia, Skyscanner and Hopper flights sort controls were never opened. The MATERIAL_CORRECTION capture itself states this outright: 'the entire flights comparison rests on Google alone' before Kayak's capture; even after Kayak it rests on two.

Thread A -- rail: Trainline has no enumerable sort-axis COUNT at all (no sort control was found on the results surface). A bar chart that puts a number next to Trainline alongside Booking.com's 11 or Google Flights' 6 would be inventing a number the capture does not provide. Only a qualitative, ordered policy statement exists for rail.

Thread A -- ranking-basis statement length: two of the seven disclosure statements collected (Kayak's per-vertical sample sentence, Tripadvisor's inline sentence) are quoted truncated, mid-word, in their own capture files. Their true character count is NOT VERIFIED and must not be estimated from the surrounding document's total length, which measures a different thing (the whole document, not the one sentence).

Thread B -- Iberia Club has no numeric tier ladder on disk at all; the page that would carry it ('Niveles Iberia Club y sus ventajas') was never opened. A four-programme tier-ladder comparison chart can only responsibly show three programmes (Booking.com, Expedia, Qatar) with real numbers; Iberia would need to be shown as a qualitative-only row or omitted, not interpolated.

Thread B -- American Airlines' AAdvantage programme has almost no data: one reward-unlock figure (15,000 Loyalty Points) and no tier names, thresholds, or benefit lists (two URL-guess 404s). It cannot be charted as a fourth or fifth full tier ladder.

Thread B -- the first-time-traveller null is confirmed for four programmes (Genius, One Key, Iberia Club, Privilege Club), not five. AAdvantage was never swept for this term set. A chart claiming '5 of 5 loyalty programmes never mention a first-time traveller' would overstate the tested sample by one.

Thread B -- Qatar's Qpoint purchase caps and minimum-earned-balance thresholds are unextracted (page returned 1,069 characters; the constraint tables did not render into text). Any 'cost to reach Silver' figure is explicitly flagged in the source as not computable, and none is reported here.

Thread C -- the five 'does a disruption route exist' results (Booking.com, Iberia, American Airlines x2, Qatar, Hopper) were produced by five different methods (site-tree category read; three-surface eleven-term sweep; URL-guess-then-read; corrected locale-matched sweep; one-surface seven-term sweep; direct navigation to a named product). None of Qatar's, Booking.com's or the AA-US result are method-matched to Iberia's, which is the only fully documented sweep. A single comparative chart ('who surfaces disruption help') would need to either restrict itself to the two method-matched tests (Iberia, Qatar's homepage sweep) or visually flag the method difference for the rest -- the source material raises this caveat explicitly and it should not be smoothed away by a chart.

Thread C -- no competitor's disruption/liability posture was tested with an actual disruption event (a real delayed or cancelled booking). Every finding here is about published statements and navigation/findability, not about what actually happens when a flight is disrupted. This is a structural limit of desk/hands-on capture, not a gap that more reading would close.

Thread D -- the two counted instances (Airbnb, Trainline) were found incidentally, not through a systematic cross-boundary test applied to all 17 competitors. The true denominator of 'how many competitors were actually tested for a boundary-state drop' is small and uneven (most competitors were never put through a matched, dated, cross-product walk the way Airbnb's stays-to-experiences and the Trainline-to-Booking.com paths were). A chart implying '2 of 17 competitors drop trip state' would misrepresent an incidental finding as a systematic measurement; the honest denominator is closer to 'of the handful of boundary crossings that were actually walked, 2 showed a drop and 2 showed data surviving intact (Kayak-to-Iberia, Iberia's fare-choice misattribution)'.
